# Planar buffered duals: face decomposition, finite facets, and analytic arcs

This is a bounded ordinary-fiber consequence of the regular buffered
dual density, with its physical freedom premise explicit. It proves
more than the existence of a separating dual, but does not assert that
an arbitrary contact-constrained mixed fiber has this freedom. An exact
disk calibration shows why the resulting analytic arcs cannot simply
be discarded.

The density and actual response are those in
`candidate a7b11eee1eaaf72e`,
Section 3. The compact submeasure martingale dual, including its proof,
is `candidate 6eda5637cc09a539`,
Section 1.

## 1. The physical freedom premise

Fix ONE actual planar fiber K=K_z and a bounded signed density Xi on
its boundary. Assume the actual response cone permits independent
deformations of this fiber with inward speed Phi|boundary K for EVERY
finite continuous convex function Phi:R^2->R, allowing Phi to have
either sign. The other fibers have zero first speed. The dual therefore
imposes

    integral_(boundary K) Xi(X) Phi(X) dS(X) <=0
                              for every such convex Phi.          (1)

Only Phi itself must be convex: the negative of a nonaffine convex
function is not presumed admissible. Constants and affine functions
of both signs are convex and are included in (1).

A sufficient geometric freedom condition is strict anchored slack:
after deleting trivial self representations, EVERY extreme anchored
inclusion in which z is a target or a positive-coefficient input has
a strictly positive support gap in every continuous unit direction.
There are finitely many extreme representations and the normal sphere
is compact, so the gaps have a common positive minimum. Every sufficiently
small Hausdorff change of K, with all other fibers fixed, remains
compatible. For each fixed signed convex Phi the actual normal-roof
body

    K_t={X:n.X+t Phi(X)<=h_K(n) for every unit n}

is convex, positive and bounded for small t>=0, is Hausdorff O(t) from
K, and has inward speed Phi at almost every old regular boundary point.
Positivity and boundedness follow from an old inner ball and a global
affine lower bound for Phi; the bounded radial first-speed argument is
the archived normal-roof construction. Thus the strict-slack condition
really supplies (1).

If such contacts are tight, (1) must NOT be inferred from the global
mixed dual by discarding its other-fiber terms. One may instead take
(1) as an explicit stronger testing hypothesis and retain its conditional
status. This is where the other-fiber constraints enter the theorem.

## 2. Exact planar boundary convex-order decomposition

Let K be any planar convex body and Xi be bounded Borel. Condition (1)
holds if and only if BOTH of the following statements hold:

(a) Xi=0 for arclength-almost every boundary point outside the relative
    interiors of the maximal nondegenerate line facets of K.

(b) On EACH such facet F, the signed measure Xi dS has zero mass,
    zero first moment along the facet, and satisfies one-dimensional
    convex order. In an arclength coordinate s in [0,l_F], this is

       integral_F Xi=0,       integral_F s Xi=0,
       integral_F (s-t)_+ Xi(s) ds <=0  for every 0<t<l_F.        (2)

This is a separate condition on each actual facet, not only on their
sum. There are at most countably many nondegenerate facets, because
their relative interiors are disjoint boundary intervals of positive
length and K has finite perimeter.

Proof of necessity. The affine tests in (1) give zero total mass and
first moment. Set mu=Xi_+ dS and nu=Xi_- dS. The nonnegative convex
tests give the compact submeasure martingale from the cited duality
theorem. Equal total mass makes its target marginal exactly nu.
Its two marginals are mutually singular.

Every boundary point outside the open line facets is an extreme point
of K. A probability measure supported in K with mean at an extreme
point is its point mass: otherwise split it into two subsets with
distinct conditional means to obtain a nontrivial convex representation.
Thus any martingale beginning at that point stays there. Mutual
singularity of mu and nu excludes such source mass.

A martingale beginning in the relative interior of a facet F stays
in its CLOSED supporting face F, by equality in the supporting linear
functional. Facet endpoints form a countable set and have zero target
arclength measure. Therefore these transports cannot send any mass
to curved/extreme boundary points, nor to the relative interior of
another facet. This proves (a) for both positive and negative parts,
and makes the transport independent on each facet. Its mass,
barycenter, and Jensen properties give (2).

Conversely (2) is the usual one-dimensional convex-order criterion:
piecewise-linear convex tests are affine functions plus nonnegative
sums of hinges, and uniform piecewise-linear approximation gives every
continuous convex test on the facet. A global finite convex Phi has
a continuous convex restriction to every facet. Sum the facet
inequalities, using boundedness on K and finite total variation;
(a) removes the remainder. This proves (1).

The same proof shows why the statement is specifically planar. In
higher dimension a curved boundary can be ruled by lower-dimensional
exposed faces carrying conditional transport along those faces. There
is no blanket curved-boundary vanishing claim in that setting.

## 3. Application to the actual buffered density

On the fixed planar fiber the regular singleton dual has the form

    Xi(X)=W(X)+G(X)+c,

    W(X)=sum_(i,j) eta_i theta_ij kappa_ij(z,X),

    G(X)=sum_i eta_i delta_i [
          1_(z=p_i) L_i(X)^(-3)/(3 E_i)
          +sum_j rho_ij (u_ij.(X-g_z))^2/(2M)],                  (3)

where c is a constant on this fiber. All eta_i,delta_i,rho_ij are
nonnegative, and the nonzero selected coefficients are positive.
Every L_i is strictly positive on a neighborhood of K. The selectors
are the actual regular closed-cap boundary selectors; positive-area
supporting ambiguity is not inserted into this formula.

There are finitely many distinct proper cap lines on this fiber with
positive coefficient in W; let their number be m. Other cap terms are
constant on the boundary. The function G is real analytic and convex
on a neighborhood of K, with Hessian

    Hess G=sum_i eta_i delta_i [
       1_(z=p_i) 4 L_i^(-5) a_i a_i^T/E_i
       +sum_j rho_ij u_ij u_ij^T/M].                            (4)

The actual source balance sum rho_ij u_ij=epsilon f_i a_i is retained.
It is not replaced by an ordinary unbuffered normal circuit.

Assume (1) for this fiber. If W is constant on a facet F, then Xi|F
is convex. The separate facet convex order allows Xi itself as its
continuous convex test, giving

    integral_F Xi^2 dS <=0.

Thus Xi vanishes identically on F. In particular its tangential
second derivative vanishes there. Formula (4) forces every positively
weighted u_ij and every present own a_i to have zero tangential
component. This conclusion needs no guessed facet-average allocation.

## 4. Finite facets and the remaining curved arcs

Suppose the quadratic matrix

    A=sum_(i,j) eta_i delta_i rho_ij u_ij u_ij^T/M

is positive definite. Then every nondegenerate facet must be crossed
in its relative interior by at least one of the m proper cap lines.
Otherwise W would be constant there, contradicting the strict
tangential curvature in (4). A proper line meets the boundary of a
convex body in at most two points unless it is a supporting line;
such a supporting line cannot cross a facet transversely. Each
crossing point lies in the interior of only one facet. Consequently

    number of nondegenerate facets <= 2m.                       (5)

After removing these finitely many closed facets and the finitely
many cap-line crossing points, each remaining boundary arc has a
constant signature W=w. Statement (a) and continuity then force

    G(X)=-c-w                                                 (6)

on that entire arc. Such a nontrivial arc is an analytic strictly
positively curved level arc. Indeed Hess G is positive definite;
grad G can vanish at at most its unique strict minimum, which cannot
contain an arc. The implicit-function theorem applies, and its
curvature is the positive tangent Hessian divided by |grad G|.

At a point joining two curved pieces with no intervening facet, G is
continuous, so the two signature constants must agree. Thus every
cap-profile jump there must cancel EXACTLY with simultaneous jumps
from other cap lines. A single positive-weight proper cap line cannot
end on the interior of such a curved arc unless another active cap
line passes through the same point with the compensating weighted
jump. This is a finite incidence restriction, not a smoothness
approximation of the body.

Equivalently, the freely variable fiber has at most 2m straight facets;
its complementary curved portions are constrained by explicit analytic
level equations and weighted crossing cancellations. If there are no
facets, W is constant around the boundary (up to its finitely many
crossings) and the WHOLE boundary lies on one level of G.

There is also a rank-one conclusion. If A has rank one, every positively
weighted continuous normal is parallel to one vector v. The source
balance makes every present own a_i parallel to v as well. Therefore
G is a strictly convex function of the one scalar v.X. Its level sets
are at most two parallel lines, so a nonflat boundary arc cannot
satisfy (6). All facets not crossed by a cap line must be parallel
to ker A; a convex body has at most two such maximal facets. The
preceding argument then gives an actual polygon with at most 2m+2
facets. This conclusion still assumes the full free-fiber test (1).

## 5. Exact curved calibration: a globally critical disk menu

Curved level arcs cannot be ruled out solely from (1)--(4), even when
the menu is an actual globally critical buffered menu. Take ONE
ordinary planar fiber K equal to the unit disk. Thus

    M=E_K(0)=pi,   Sigma=I/4,   f(0)=1,   epsilon=1.

Choose three unit vectors n_j at angles 0,2pi/3,4pi/3 and put

    u_j=2 n_j,   Gamma(u_j)=1,   rho_j=theta_j=1/3,
    H_j={u_j.X>=-1}={n_j.X>=-1/2}.

The own buffered sections are proper and regular. Each cap has

    Q=2pi/3+sqrt(3)/4,
    beta=2/3+sqrt(3)/(4pi),
    S_j=sqrt(3)/2,
    B=sum rho_j/S_j=2/sqrt(3),
    delta=epsilon f/B=sqrt(3)/2.                               (7)

The actual buffered maximum is uniquely at zero. At zero every unit
continuous direction has the cap mass Q. For any nonzero mark y,
take the unit direction y/|y|. Since f(y)<=1, its buffered threshold
is |y|-f(y)/2>-1/2, so its captured area is strictly below Q.
The pure-base value in rank zero is the full mass. Thus these are
genuine globally minimizing cap directions at the unique deepest
buffered mark, not an arbitrary imposed profile.

On the circle, away from the three intersections of cap lines,
exactly two caps contain each point. Hence W=2/3 almost everywhere.
The projective parameter is a=0, the balance sum rho u=0=epsilon f a
is exact, and

    sum_j rho_j(u_j.X)^2=2|X|^2.

The actual density (4) in the physical-response source therefore is,
on |X|=1,

    Xi=2/3-beta
          +delta[1/(3pi)+2/(2pi)-5/(6pi)]
       =2/3-beta+sqrt(3)/(4pi)=0.                              (8)

It annihilates EVERY boundary speed, and in particular every signed
convex-potential test. The quadratic matrix is positive definite.
The circle is exactly the allowed analytic level curve; the profile
jumps cancel at the three shared chord endpoints.

This is NOT a bad-depth or attained-shape-minimum example. Its depth
is safely above gamma_2, and epsilon=1 is not the arbitrarily small
buffer parameter of the outer bad-minimum construction. It shows
precisely that the dual density's algebraic form plus actual criticality
does not by itself imply polygonality. A further bad-depth or
quantitative small-buffer input, or the constrained mixed contact
structure, is still required for such an exclusion.

## 6. What is new and what remains conditional

The new bounded consequence is the exact planar face-by-face dual
decomposition, its finite-facet bound, and its analytic arc/incidence
restriction for the actual Xi density. It is not another separation
statement. The disk is an exact obstruction to strengthening it to
unconditional exclusion of curved arcs.

The full mixed dual tests compatible arrays, not an independently
free fiber. Tight anchored contacts can fund a fiber's positive
response with negative responses elsewhere, and then (1) may fail
even though the global dual is valid. Extending this theorem through
those labeled contacts requires an additional geometric argument;
none is assumed here.
## 7. A quantitative small-buffer exclusion with the dual labels retained

Normalize the dual weights by sum_i eta_i=1, and let s be their positive
support size. Put

    Delta=sum_i eta_i delta_i.

For ANY particular source p_i whose fiber has no line facet and enjoys
the independent freedom of Section 1, the exact density gives

    beta >= eta_i/2 - 5 Delta/(6M).                              (9)

Here the other witness profiles and quadratic terms are retained; none
is dropped with the wrong sign. Indeed on this fiber

    Xi=W+G-beta-5 Delta/(6M),     G>=0,
    W=sum_l eta_l W_l >= eta_i W_i.

The own source y_i is interior and every own selected buffered cap has
strictly negative threshold relative to y_i. Along any generic pair
of opposite rays from y_i, at least one boundary endpoint belongs to
each cap. Consequently the two values of W_i sum to at least 1, and
one is at least 1/2. Choose the rays away from the finitely many proper
cap-line crossing points. Since there are no facets, Section 2 makes
Xi vanish almost everywhere, and continuity on each fixed-signature
arc makes it vanish at the chosen endpoint. The displayed inequalities
then prove (9). Equivalently, one can choose a full-measure set of rays:
radial projection from an interior point preserves boundary null sets
because it is bi-Lipschitz on a planar convex body's boundary.

In particular, for a single selected witness this says

    beta >= 1/2 - 5 delta/(6M).                                 (10)

If EVERY positive-weight witness source fiber is freely variable and
has no facets, choose an index with eta_i>=1/s. This yields

    beta >= 1/(2s) - 5 Delta/(6M).                              (11)

There is a direct uniform version on the normalized compact family.
With Gamma_C(u)=sqrt(u^T Sigma u)=1, let

    Smax = [sum_z max_(|v|=1,c) length(K_z intersect {v.X=c})]
                                      *sqrt(lambda_max(Sigma)).

Every actual total coarea S_ij is at most Smax: |u_ij| is at least
1/sqrt(lambda_max(Sigma)), and the ordinary section lengths are
bounded by the displayed maximum. Since sum_j rho_ij=1,

    B_i=sum_j rho_ij/S_ij >=1/Smax,
    delta_i=epsilon f_i/B_i <=epsilon Smax,                     (12)

where f_i=(E_i/M)^(1/3)<=1. Thus Delta<=epsilon Smax.
If s<=k and beta<gamma_2/k, gamma_2=4/9, then for

    epsilon < M/(15 k Smax)                                    (13)

the right side of (11) is strictly greater than gamma_2/k, a
contradiction. More precisely, already a maximum-weight witness
eta_i>=1/s cannot simultaneously have independent freedom and a
facetless source fiber under (13). At least that witness must have
a nontrivial flat boundary segment or fail the stated independent
freedom premise.

This is the concrete local structural alternative. It is not a claim
that every fiber is polygonal, that an arbitrary contact-constrained
fiber is free, or that the nonregular allocation problem is solved.
A tight anchored contact can invalidate the free-fiber test; a line
facet can carry the nonzero one-dimensional transport in Section 2.
Those are the two remaining geometric mechanisms in this lemma.
